messages.body_plain:

messages.subject: Re: statistical question
messages.body_plain:
With no more information than what you have provided, we can consider 
only the population from which your participants can be assumed to be a 
random sample. If random numbers were not used appropriately in the 
selection of participants, your results could be an artifact of the 
selection process. Part of this is knowing if these 41 were each 
selected individually. If, for example, you visited a Center for X and 
interviewed all 41 individuals who happened to be available that day, 
then your real sample size at one level is 1 center, not 41 individuals, 
unless you are only interested in that 1 center. If you visited 3 
different Centers and interviewed, say, 12, 15, and 14 people at the 3 
centers, totaling 41, and you want to know about people at these types 
of centers generally, then you have a "components of variance" question.

For simplicity, I will assume that you contacted 41 centers from a 
longer list of such centers, selected one person at random at each of 
those centers and collected data on that person -- and no one refused to 
cooperate. Let p = the proportion of people in the "certain population" 
who are insecure. Then the probability that all n of a sample of n were 
insecure is p^n. Thus, if 50% of you population is insecure, then the 
probability of getting 100% insecure in a sample of 41 is 0.5^41 = 
5e-13. Similarly, if only 90% are insecure, then the probability of 
getting 41 of 41 insecure = 0.9^41 = 0.013. As an intuitive check on 
this, we can also compute the probability of getting 0 insecure people 
in a sample of 41 from a population with 90% insecure = probability of 
41 secure = (1-0.9)^41 = 1e-41.

By an extension of this argument, we can compute a 95% confidence 
interval for the proportion of people who are insecure in the population 
for which your data can be considered a random sample: Since 100% of the 
sample were insecure, it is clear that the upper bound of the interval 
should be 1, i.e., we need a 1-sided confidence interval (in the absence 
of other information, of course). The lower bound will be the proportion 
p for which p^41 = 0.05, for which p = 0.05^(1/41) = 0.93. In other 
words, with 95% confidence, we can say that the the proportion of 
insecure people in that population is at least 93%.

What other data did you collect on these people? If, for example, you 
used a standard questionnaire with a known distribution of the scores, 
then you can say more using that distribution.

hope this helps.
spencer graves

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone!

 

I need to compare two
regression models: 

The first model is

 

Y = b0 + b1*X + b2*Z + b3*XZ

 

where XZ is the product of the two predictors X and Z.

The second model is derived
from the first by the

following nonlinear constraint:

 

b1 = -mean(Z)*b3

 

where mean(Z) is the estimated mean of Z.

So the second model is specified
by

 

Y = b0 + (-mean(Z)*b3) * X + b2*Z + b3*XZ

 

The comparison of these two
models should be

tested with a likelihood ratio test.

Can anyone give me a hint if
this is possible in S-Plus?

 

Felix Flory

University of Jena, Germany

messages.subject: Re: Compare two regression models etc.
messages.body_plain:
OK --- if it's thesis work, consider this to be a consultation.
(No charge, of course!)

It seems to me that the problem is quite simple; you need to
consider two cases:

Case 1: Z.bar not equal to 0.

(I'm denoting by ``Z.bar'' what you referred to as ``mean(Z)''.

You then have:

        Model 1: Y = c_0 + c_1*(Z.bar*X) + c_2*Z + c_3*Z*X + E

        Model 2: Y = c_0 - c_3*(Z.bar*X) + c_2*Z + c_3*Z*X + E

(I've changed the names of the coefficients from ``b'' to ``c''
for a reason, which you will see below.)

I.e. Model 2 is obtained from Model 1 by the (linear) constraint

                c_1 = -c_3

Hence Model 2 is linearly nested in Model 1 and the usual linear
model hypothesis testing can be carried out.

But, I hear you cry out, Model 1 is NOT the ``Model 1'' that
I had in mind, which was

        Model 1': Y = b_0 + b_1*X + b_2*Z + b_3*Z*X + E

Ah, but Model 1 and Model 1' are ***the same*** provided Z.bar is
not 0.  Simply set

                c_0 = b_0
                c_1 = b_1/Z.bar
                c_2 = b_2
                c_3 = b_3

and you have the same thing.  The division by Z.bar is where you
require Z.bar not equal to 0.

The key thing to recognize is that if you want the term
``-b_3*Z.bar*X'' in the model, where b_3 is to be a fitted
coefficient, then Z.bar*X is one of the ***predictors*** in the
model.  And if you are hypothesizing about the coefficient of that
predictor, then that predictor must appear in both models.  (Unless
of course you are hypothesizing that the coefficient is 0.  See
below.)

Case 2:  Z.bar equals 0.

In this case the two models are

        Model 1: Y = c_0 + c_1*X + c_2*Z + c_3*Z*X + E

        Model 2: Y = c_0 + c_2*Z + c_3*Z*X + E

i.e. you simply want to test the hypothesis that c_1 = 0, which is
again a standard linear model hypothesis test.

                                cheers,

                                        Rolf Turner
                                        rolf at math.unb.ca

messages.subject: Re: Compare two regression models etc.
messages.body_plain:
Thank you again so much.

My simulation studies clearly show, that if the population mean
Z.bar of the covariate Z is estimated, the glm test fails to
compare the two models. Or: which is identical to test the 
hypothesis: b1 = -Z.bar*b3.  

The two models can be compared however using the likelihood
ratio test with nonlinear constraints (since model two has 
a product of two parameters to estimate). This test is
implemented in Lisrel8.54 and provides perfect results.
So my question is, if S-Plus can also do this test:
a likelihood ratio test with a nonlinear 
constraint (the hypothesis).

Felix Flory
University of Jena, Germany

Erin,

I am not seeing some lines I expected in the nmake command, in particular 
no line to make EZAP.obj and no line to make S.def.  Had you made some

The thing to do is to find out what S.dll actually exports, using

dumpbin /exports S.dll

at the command prompt.  If ezap_ is there, fine.  If perchance EZAP_ is 
there, use "EZAP" in your .Fortran call. If neither is, start the chapter 
again, in a clean directory (or at least remove chapter.mif).

Caveats: I don't have 6.2, and I don't know what exact compiler versions 
etc you are using.

messages.subject: SHORT COURSE: Bayesian hierarchical modeling, 26 Mar 2004
messages.subject_clean: SHORT COURSE: Bayesian hierarchical modeling, 26 Mar 2004
messages.body_plain:
Greetings, and apologies for cross-posting.

If you would please make the following announcement known to any 
colleagues, students, etc., who may be interested, that would be 
terrific.

Many thanks and best wishes, David Draper

2004 American Statistical Association LearnSTAT Program Offering:

Title: Intermediate/Advanced Bayesian Hierarchical Modeling

Date: 26 March 2004

Instructor: David Draper
            Department of Applied Mathematics and Statistics
            University of California, Santa Cruz

Summary: An award-winning short course on intermediate- and
advanced-level methods and applications of Bayesian hierarchical
modeling, including (a) reviews of Bayesian modeling, Bayesian
computation, and hierarchical models (HMs) for meta-analysis, and (b)
coverage of (1) Bayesian model diagnostics, model checking, and model
elaboration; (2) mixture modeling with latent variables; (3) HMs for
clustered (hierarchical, multilevel) data; and (4) semi-parametric HMs
for dealing realistically with model uncertainty. Case studies drawn from
medicine, education, and environmental risk assessment.

One-day course: 6 hours of material covered in an 8-hour time slot, with
30 minutes of breaks in each of the morning and afternoon sessions and a
one-hour break for lunch

Location: Arlington Campus Professional Center
          George Mason University
          3401 North Fairfax Drive
          Arlington, Virginia
          (Near Washington, DC)

Registration Fee: $500 for ASA members
                  $600 for nonmembers

(Registration fee includes 225 pages of materials, lunch, and
refreshments for AM and PM breaks)

Registration Deadline: March 5, 2004

Register Online at:    www.amstat.org/education

Abstract:

This course provides coverage of intermediate- and advanced-level topics
arising in the formulation, fitting, and checking of hierarchical or
multilevel models from the Bayesian point of view. The Bayesian approach
is particularly effective in fitting hierarchical models because other
model-based methods -- principally involving maximum likelihood -- often
do not capture all relevant sources of uncertainty, leading to
over-confident decisions and scientific conclusions.

The basic principles of Bayesian hierarchical modeling are reviewed in
this course with emphasis on practical rather than theoretical issues. 
Intermediate- and advanced-level ideas are illustrated with real data
drawn from case studies involving complicated applications of
hierarchical models in cluster sampling and mixture modeling. The course
is intended for applied statisticians with an interest in learning more
about intermediate and advanced topics in hierarchical modeling in
general, and the Bayesian analysis of such models in particular.

Instructor:

David Draper is a Professor in, and Chair of, the Department of Applied
Mathematics and Statistics in the Baskin School of Engineering at the
University of California, Santa Cruz. From 2001 to 2003 he served as the
President-Elect, President, and Past President of the International
Society for Bayesian Analysis (ISBA). His research is in the areas of
Bayesian inference and prediction, model uncertainty and empirical
model-building, hierarchical modeling, Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods,
and Bayesian semi-parametric methods, with applications mainly in health
policy, education, and environmental risk assessment. When he gave this
same short course at the San Francisco JSM last year, it won the ASA
Excellence in Continuing Education award for 2003. He has received or
been nominated for major teaching awards everywhere he has taught
(University of Chicago; RAND Graduate School of Public Policy; University
of California, Los Angeles; University of Bath (U.K.); and University of
California, Santa Cruz). He has a particular interest in the exposition
of complex statistical methods and ideas in the context of real-world
applications.

For more information and to register for this course, visit the Education
section of the ASA Web site at www.amstat.org/education and click on the
link for this course.

Questions? email LearnSTAT at amstat.org or call (+1) (703) 684-1221 ext.
166.

messages.subject: How to code this?
messages.body_plain:
Imagine a regression setting with p explanatory variables. There are to 
2^p possible models (intercept always included), each of which can be 
represented by a sequence of T and F, according to the inclusion of the 
corresponding variable in the model. One can then build a matrix with 
2^p rows and p columns representing all possible models.

For example, if p=4 I have the following matrix:

> allmodels
     [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
[1,]    F    F    F    F
[2,]    F    F    F    T
[3,]    F    F    T    F
[4,]    F    T    F    F
[5,]    T    F    F    F
[6,]    F    F    T    T
[7,]    F    T    F    T
[8,]    F    T    T    F
[9,]    T    F    F    T
[10,]    T    F    T    F
[11,]    T    T    F    F
[12,]    F    T    T    T
[13,]    T    F    T    T
[14,]    T    T    F    T
[15,]    T    T    T    F
[16,]    T    T    T    T

For a given model mod (for example mod = c(F,T,T,F)), I need to 
construct the submatrix of allmodels that contains all the possible 
models with either an additional variable or one variable less. In the 
case of mod, I would like to get

> submodels
     [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
[1,]    F    F    T    F
[2,]    F    T    F    F
[3,]    F    T    T    T
[4,]    T    T    T    F

Any idea on how to code this in a general manner?

Thank you for your help,

Eva Cantoni

count of bumblebees along various transects. The explanatory 
variables are habitat type (factor with 6 levels), number of flowers 
(continuous), temperature (continuous) and wind speed (continuous). The 
transects are different lengths so I?m trying to use an offset:

glm(bees ~ habitat*flowers + temp + wind, family = poisson,

I think it must have something to do with my missing values, because I've

tom

messages.body_plain:
If you take a look at the help page for offset, I 
think the standard approach

is to include it in the model formula.  I 
tried a small example and it seemed

to take care of the problem. I think the model 
formula is used to determine 

the X matrix, so if the offset has missing values, 
that information has to be

processed at the time the X matrix is 
generated.

 

Simple test:

 

glm(1:10 ~ rnorm(10), offset=c(1:9,NA), 
na.action="">

glm(1:10 ~ rnorm(10) + offset(c(1:9,NA)), 
na.action="">

The first fails but the second works.

 

Pete

Bert, D. Rizopoulos, T. Burr, S. Buttrey, P. Ilouga, E. Hodgess, N. Ellis).

The fact that I didn't specify the final goal of my project (it would 
have been very long) let some of you think that I was reinventing 
wheels. The piece of code I'm writing will be part of a model selection 
appraoch for longitudinal models (using cross-validation and MCMC). 
Therefore, the function leaps() that does all possible subsets 
regression (for linear models) is not suitable in my case. As pointed 
out, the function subsets() from Venables's and Ripley's S-PROGRAMMING 
(p. 49) can be used to obtain all possible subsets and this (or a 
similar version) is what I used to produce the allmodels matrix. add1() 
and drop1() functions have methods for lm and aov only (?).

I like the following solution (which is short and easy to understand):

model <- c(F,T,T,F)

submodel <- matrix(rep(model,p),nrow=p,ncol=p) 
# there will always be p submodels because change one F or T at a time

diag(submodel) <- !diag(submodel) # switch one F to T or one T to F per row.

Listed below are the other proposals I received with my comments, and at 
the end of the message, the original query.

Thank you again,
Eva Cantoni

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

submat <- t(matrix(rep(mod,p),p))
for (i=1:p) {
submat[i,i] <- 1 - submat[i,i]
}

I probably have some syntax wrong, but the general idea is that you have 
p copies of mat, each is "one-off" from the original, the one-off being 
the "not" of the original.

  if(nna==n && na==1) y <- 1 else y <- 0

  if(nna==(n-1) && na==0) w <- 1 else w <- 0

  y+w

}, mod, n)

allmodels[index==1,]

flopper
function(vec)

        out <- matrix(rep(vec, each = length(vec)), length(vec), length(vec))

        out
}

if your vector has length n, "flopper" creates an nxn matrix of copies of the input. Then it changes each row in one position by logically NOT-ting the diagonal.

messages.subject: linear models problem
messages.body_plain:
I have a question concerning linear models. I have measured the effect of
time on a response variable y. Furthermore, data are from several
experimental groups. My primary question was simply to test if time had
an effect on the response variable and if the slopes differed between
groups. This is no problem. My major problem is that there seem to be a
"time lag" before one sees an effect on y (y can only have
values > 0). My second aim was to test if this hypothetical time lag
is significantly different from zero and further to test if the time lag
differed between groups. In my naivety, I thought that different
y-intercept would tell me this. But, even if all groups have the same
time lag, if slopes differ so will the y-intercept. 

I assume my model could be written as: 

y = b*(x-x0)+error 

in which b and x0 can differ between groups.

How is it possible to test this model in S-Plus?

I want to test the following hypotheses: 

Is b>0 (it is)? 
Does b differ between groups? 
Is x0 > 0? 
Does x0 differ between groups? 

 Thanks 

Leif Engqvist

I

messages.subject: Re: Postscript function
messages.body_plain:
Have you overwritten it or just masked it?  Have you tried 
"masked()" and "conflicts()"? 

     To actually overwrite it, you would have to either (a) "attach" 
the "splus" directory to the first position in the search path before 
replacing it with a standard assign operation or (b) use the "assign" 
function.  If you just masked it, then "rm(postscript)" should make the 
standard function available again.  If you actually overwrote it, you 
could try replacing it with a copy of the S-Plus code obtained from 
someone else.  In the latter case, you might try the "postscript" 
function copied below from S-Plus 6.2.  If that fails, then I would 
reinstall S-Plus. 

     hope this helps. 
     spencer graves

> postscript
function(file = NULL, width = -1, height = -1, append = F, onefile = T,
   print.it = NULL, ...)
{
   .ps.options <- lapply(ps.options(), eval)
   xtras <- list(...)
   if(length(xtras) > 0) {
       # Normalize the names.
       .names <- names(xtras)
       .full.names <- names(.ps.options)
       .matched <- charmatch(.names, .full.names, nomatch = 0)
       .names[.matched > 0] <- paste("ps.", .full.names[.matched],
           sep = "")
       .full.names <- paste("ps.", .full.names, sep = "")
       .matched <- charmatch(.names, .full.names, nomatch = 0)
       .names[.matched > 0] <- .full.names[.matched]
       .dup <- duplicated(.names)
       if(any(.dup)) {
           for(i in names(xtras)[.dup])
               warning(paste("Discarding duplicate option:",
                   i))
           xtras <- xtras[!.dup]
           names(xtras) <- .names[!.dup]
       }
       else names(xtras) <- .names
   }
   if(!is.null(xtras$ps.defaults))
       .ps.options <- xtras$ps.defaults
   .paper <- if(!is.null(xtras$ps.paper)) xtras$ps.paper else .ps.options$
           paper
   .paper <- casefold(.paper)
   .pointsize <- if(is.null(xtras$ps.pointsize)) .ps.options$pointsize
        else xtras$ps.pointsize
   .region <- if(is.null(xtras$ps.region)) .ps.options$region else xtras$
           ps.region
   if(length(.region) == 1 && .region == -1) {
       if(exists("ps.paper.regions")) {
           .reg.names <- casefold(dimnames(ps.paper.regions)[[
               1]])
           .idx <- match(.paper, .reg.names)
           if(!is.na(.idx))
               .region <- ps.paper.regions[.idx,  ]
       }
   }
   .horizontal <- if(is.null(xtras$ps.horizontal)) .ps.options$horizontal
        else xtras$ps.horizontal
   if(missing(print.it))
       print.it <- -1
   else if(is.logical(print.it))
       print.it <- if(print.it) 1 else 0
   n <- nchar(.paper)
   if(missing(width))
       width <- .ps.options$width
   if(missing(height))
       height <- .ps.options$height
   tpar <- c(width, height, .horizontal, print.it, .pointsize, rep(
       .region, length = 4), n)
   if(n > 0)
       tpar <- c(tpar, as.single(AsciiToInt(.paper)))
   n <- if(is.null(file)) 0 else nchar(file)
   tpar <- c(tpar, n)
   if(n > 0)
       tpar <- c(tpar, as.single(AsciiToInt(file)))
   argv <- c(list(name = "postscript", pars = as.single(tpar), npars =
       length(tpar)), xtras)
   do.call("pipegraph", argv)
   .C("S_send_ps_int",
       as.integer(if(append) 1 else 0),
       as.character("la"))
   .C("S_send_ps_int",
       as.integer(if(onefile) 1 else 0),
       as.character("lo"))
   invisible()
}

messages.subject: spatial GLMM with nested correlation structure
messages.subject_clean: spatial GLMM with nested correlation structure
messages.body_plain:
Hello all -- I'm in the midst of modeling the distribution of
ice-hauling seals in relation to covariates such as  day of year (DOY)
and ice cover (ICE.COV).  By strip-transect sampling on 20 separate
days, I have created a lattice of cells containing seal counts and the
corresponding covariate measures.  To remove a significant north-south
trend in seal counts, I extracted the residuals from a GAM loess smooth
of seal counts on the lat/long variables. Modeling the residuals, I
arrived at the following best fit (using AIC):

glmmPQL(sealsum.gamfit ~ ICE.COV * DOY * VAR3 * VAR4, random = ~ 1| DOY,

family = poisson, data = grid.gamfit, correlation = corGaus(form = ~
lat + lon | DOY), verbose = T))

I determined that a gaussian variogram best fit the spatial
autocorrelation by exploring the data in Surfer, VarioWin, and S+.  But
I have encountered a significant degree of both geometric and zonal
anisotropy.  I believe the anisotropy is real as there are several
reasonable hypothesis that explain its presence which have to do with
the seals concentrating in a stream of ice, i.e., creating
discontinuities in variance and correlation within the study area.
Though less than ideal, I have been able to model the autocorrelation
(in
VarioWin) by nesting two spatial structures (both Gaussian)
corresponding to the directions of maximum and minimum continuity.  The
problem is that I now need to transport this nested model into the S+
spatial GLMM framework.  The avenues I have explored thus far are:

1)  create a new corStruct class in S+ that corresponds to a
gaussian-gaussian nested model.  Problem:  I have been unable to find
an adequate explanation of the steps to create a new corStruct class
though the online help indicates that it is possible.

2)  transforming/weighting the coordinates prior to running the model.
Problem:  though a geometric transform of the coordinates is
straightforward it is less obvious how to conduct such a transform using

a nested model.

It may be I'm forcing a square peg (nested model) in a round hole (S+
spatial GLMM), but I'm hoping someone out there has done this in S+
before and can pass along their experience.  Otherwise, I'm soliciting
the wisdom of those who know where to find the square hole that matches
my square peg, i.e., other software or techniques that allow one to
account for spatial correlation with nested structures with the main
focus of modeling the relation of animals to their environment.  Much
gratitude for any assistance.  Thanks,  John Jansen

ps.  I'm using Splus 6.1, MASS and S+ spatial
--
John K. Jansen
Wildlife Biologist
National Marine Mammal Laboratory
NOAA Fisheries
7600 Sand Point Way N.E.  Bldg 4
Seattle, WA 98115-6349

fax: 206.526.6615

messages.subject: coxph() with simultaneously occuring time-dependant events
messages.subject_clean: coxph() with simultaneously occuring time-dependant events
messages.body_plain:
Dear S-news readers,

I have the following question concerning the use of coxph() with 
time-dependant covariates. I am analyzing the duration of a behavior in 
animals, and want to understand the effect of the number of two types of 
events A & B appearing during the behavior studied.

Using the "counting process formulation" proposed by T.M. Therneau, this 
can be handled rather easily.

Lets take an example, in which we have the following observation (where the 
ti are different observed times):

0 (beginning) -------> t1 (A) ------> t2 (B) -------> t3 (A) -------> t4 
(end of behavior, not right-censored)

Such a situation can/should be coded that way:

start    stop    A     B      cens
     0       t1    0      0           0
    t1       t2    1      0           0
    t2       t3    1      1           0
    t3       t4    2      1           1

and then with:  coxph(Surv(start, stop, cens) ~ A + B)

This works fine, and enables indeed to estimate the effect of the two 
events, separately.

Now, in my case the two events A & B are:

1) Only two possible situations that are mutually exclusive (i.e., coming 
from a binomial process).

2) Either observed or sometimes estimated with probability "p" and "1-p".

For example, suppose that (1) event A is "encountering a strong competitor" 
and event B is "encountering a weak competitor", (2) there are only two 
types of competitors, and (3) the status of the competitor can sometimes 
only be estimated with probability.

Thus, as an example, consider again the situation given above, but suppose 
that, at time t2, we can only know the probability p of having an event A 
(or, equivalently, the probability (1-p) of have an event B). The two 
events A at time t1 & t3 are known to be A.

My question is then: How should the date be coded to fit a Cox's model?

I would say like this:

start    stop       A                B       cens
     0       t1        0                0           0
    t1       t2        1                0           0
    t2       t3    1+p          (1-p)           0
    t3       t4    2+p          (1-p)           1

Is this ok? What worries me is that there are two covariates whose values 
are changing at time t2 (this is why I place the word "simultaneously" in 
the title of this question), and this is thus not strictly following a 
"counting process formulation" anymore. Any idea on this will be welcomed.

Thanks!

messages.subject: Re: Nevermind: Desktop Locks When S-Plus is Busy
messages.subject_clean: Nevermind: Desktop Locks When S-Plus is Busy
messages.body_plain:
I would have to disagree . . . in the current (i.e. 32-bit) Windows 
operating systems such as Windows 2000 and XP, NOT all applications behave 
this way (as the original poster mentioned with Illustrator) especially if 
you lower the process priority. I have had major processing jobs (including 
a large model run with SPSS 10.0) running in the background for over a week 
while still maintaining full use of my computer, although sometimes at 
reduced speed. This program-to-program variation likely has to do with how 
well applications processes are written to handle multi-threading. Thus any 
performance hits or stability problems encountered when running background 
tasks with S-PLUS are more likely the fault of S-PLUS itself.

With the introduction of hyperthreading processors such as the new Pentium 
4's, I expect that many more applications will be written with this in mind 
and will thus allow more stable and efficient "true" multitasking.

My $0.02.
Stephen

messages.subject_clean: Problem with loess call in functions
messages.body_plain:
Hi John,

Your problem is caused by the scooping rules.  The following will work and
.tmp.dat will not exist when loess.fitter returns.  I think 'get(...)' can
just be replaced by '.tmp.dat', but 'get' is used as an extra precaution.

"loess.fitter" <-
function(x, y, xnew, span)
{
        dat <- data.frame(y=y, x=x)
        assign(".tmp.dat", dat, frame=1)
        lo.model <- loess(y ~ x, span = span,
                          data = get(".tmp.dat", frame=1))
        lo.pred <- predict(lo.model, xnew, se.fit = T)
        lines(xnew, lo.pred$fit, col = 2, lwd = 3)
        lo.ci <- pointwise(lo.pred)
        lines(xnew, lo.ci$lower, col = 2, lwd = 3)
        lines(xnew, lo.ci$upper, col = 2, lwd = 3)
}

Regards,
Henrik

messages.body_plain:
I've gotten similar problems in the past.  I've handled them by 
passing 0.5*(txx1+t(txx1)) instead of txx1 to chol or whatever the 
offending function was. 

     However, if you are actually doing this computation, you are 
better off using the QR decomposition on x1 than the choleski 
decomposition on txx1, because you lose half of the digits in numerical 
precision with the latter computation.  To see this, note that if the 
singular values of txx1 are the squares of those of x1: 

> svd(x1)$d
[1] 10.626920  9.775804  9.504342
> svd(txx1)$d
[1] 112.93143  95.56635  90.33252

     Therefore, the ratio of the smallest to the largest singular 
values of txx1 is the square of that of x1.  In a different problem, if 
the ratio of the smallest singular value to the largest for x1 is 1e-9, 
then that same ratio for txx1 is 1e-18.  It can still be computed from 
x1, but it is smaller than round-off from txx1.  This can easily happen 
with larger dimensions unless one is extremely careful with scaling. 

     hope this helps. 
     spencer graves

messages.subject: Re: t(x)%*%x is non-symmetric in S-plus 6.1 on P4 Dual
messages.subject_clean: t(x)%*%x is non-symmetric in S-plus 6.1 on P4 Dual
messages.body_plain:
As far as I know, this problem occurs because the fast compiled version of 
t(x) %*% x can produce a matrix that is non-symmteric on the order of 
machine epsilon.  (I would guess this is due to keeping some intermediate 
results in the 80 bit hardware FP registers).  The fortran function that 
chol() calls does not tolerate these insignificant deviations from the 
symmetric.

The fix that I have been using successfully since March 25, 2003, is to use 
the S-plus function choleski() -- the Fortran function that it calls does 
not appear to be affected by the deviations from the symmetric that are in 
the result of t(x) %*% x.  The interface to choleski() is different than 
chol(), but it's not that difficult to cope with.

The other fix is to make the result of z <- t(x) %*% x symmetric.  One way 
to to compute (z + t(z))/2.

-- Tony Plate

messages.subject: Re: Nevermind: Desktop Locks When S-Plus is Busy
messages.subject_clean: Nevermind: Desktop Locks When S-Plus is Busy
messages.body_plain:
Stephen Ban writes:

> This program-to-program variation likely has to do with how 
> well applications processes are written to handle multi-threading.
> Thus any performance hits or stability problems encountered when 
> running background tasks with S-PLUS are more likely the fault
> of S-PLUS itself.

I'd counter your suggestion with the observation that S-PLUS works just fine
running in conjunction with other applications on other operating systems
such as Linux and Solaris without unduly affecting the performance of the S's
GUI. Even amongst different versions of the Windows operating systems, their
configurations ("perfomance optimization" settings), there is significant
variability.

> With the introduction of hyperthreading processors such as 
> the new Pentium 4's, I expect that many more applications will be written 
> with this in mind and will thus allow more stable and efficient "true"
> multitasking.

A warning about hyperthreading: while making a single processor behave "like"
multiple logical processors can improve the perceived performance of desktop
applications (like Word, Outlook, Excel) which typically don't require much
processing power, you still only have one *real* CPU.  As a result,
applications which require heavy processing power like S-PLUS (which will
often run at 100% CPU utilization) do not benefit from hyperthreading.  In
fact, anecdotal evidence suggests that enabling hyperthreading can in fact
*hinder* the performance of compute-intensive applications.

I often have compute-bound S-plus jobs using up both of my CPUs on a dual 
Xeon workstation running Windows 2000.  I find I can almost always get 
quite decent interactive performance from other applications if I set the 
priority of the S-plus processes to "Below Normal" or "Low" in the 
"Processes" tab of the Windows Task manager -- get the appropriate menu by 
right-clicking on the process.  Still, just several times per day, response 
for interactive processes is painfully slow. Possibly, my different 
experience to Kim's (in that reducing priority of the S-plus process helps) 
is due to my having sufficient memory -- I have 4GB of physical memory.

-- Tony Plate

Fortran code which:

messages.body_plain:
I wish to thank everyone on their thoughts about this.  There is apparently 
nothing amiss here as this behavior is expected. It is an irritation when 
S-Plus needs to crank on something for a few hours as I have a dual-Athlon 
workstation and see that S-Plus can only use one of the processors at a 
time.  Still, reducing S-Plus's execution priority to Below Norman and Low 
does seem to help, and I will continue to do that. Memory availability 
isn't an issue, as I have 2 GB of RAM which is all that Windows, being a 32 
bit OS, can address.

Aside from some matrix operations, and apparently the old Matrix library, a 
truly multi-threaded version of S-Plus would be welcome for those of us 
lucky enough to have dual-processor machines.

Thanks again to all on the list!

Kim Elmore

        Cooperative Institute for Mesoscale Meteorological Studies

Regarding my first question, 

I would like to thank Bert Gunter, Sam Buttrey, Scott Chasalow, and Patrick
Burns, all who alerted me to the fact that I need to call upon
"NLSstRtAsymptote.sortedXyData" to determine the algorithm for the
NLSstRtAsymptote() function.

With respect to the second question (which can be found at the bottom of this
email) regarding the nls.control() option when using the SSasymp self-start
function within nls(), I would greatly appreciate any leads/suggestions for
determining the answer to this. 

Thank you, 

Joe Rausch

You need to ask for the specific method for the sortedXyData class (as is stated
in the Help file).
 
 NLSstRtAsymptote.sortedXyData
function(xy)
{
 ## Is the last response value closest to the minimum or to
 ## the maximum?
 in.range <- range(xy$y)
 last.dif <- abs(in.range - xy$y[nrow(xy)])
 ## Estimate the asymptote as the largest (smallest) response
 ## value plus (minus) 1/8 of the range. 
 if(match(min(last.dif), last.dif) == 2) {
  return(in.range[2] + diff(in.range)/8)
 }
 in.range[1] - diff(in.range)/8
}

Cheers,
Bert

How about the following: 

DF <- data.frame(a=1:3, b=4:6)

DF. <- data.frame(lapply(DF, function(x)x/sqrt(sum(x^2))))

lapply(DF., function(x)sum(x^2))

CD <- function(X)
{
       p <- dim(X)[2]
       normx <- vector()
        UX <- X
       for(a in 1:p) {
               normx[a] <- vecnorm(X[, a])
                 UX[,a] <- X[,a]/normx[a]
       }
       return(UX)
}
CD(DF)

all.equal(DF., CD(DF))

hope this helps. 
spencer graves

messages.subject: mixed effects model
messages.body_plain:
Dear list members,

I´ve fitted a LME to data consisting of a mix of categorical and numeric 
variables in data from a split-plot experiment.

consumption is the response

A, B are integer variables

treatment is a 2-level factor

biomass is a numeric variable (non-integers allowed) and is assumed to 
be a covariate of A (it is assumed that A is linearly correlated with 
biomass)

startsize is a numeric variable (non-integers allowed) and is a 
covariate of consumption (it is assumed that size at start of the 
experiment influences consumption)

block and treatment are random effects

The model I used then looks like this:
model1_lme(consumption~block+A+B+treatment+biomass+startsize,data=DATA,random=~1|block/treatment)

Do you think that a model structure like this (with that kind of mixture 
between numeric and categorical variables) is appropriate? I especially 
wonder if it´s allowed to include covariates in the form I did it.

Thanks very much for any suggestions
Chris.

messages.subject: Re: Capturing script name
messages.body_plain:
Assignments you make inside a script to frame 1 will persist during the 
execution of a script, if I'm not mistaken. So if you add a line like

assign ("current.script", "name.of.this.script", frame=1)

to the top of each script, with the appropriate script name in the second 
argument, you'll be able to find that inside the script.

For example, put this in a script:

assign ("current.script", "name.of.this.script", frame=1)
plot(1:5, 1:5, main = "Five Dots!")
mtext (paste ("Produced by", current.script))

But I don't know how you can capture the file name of the script directly. In 
particular some scripts (ones you've created during this session) haven't been 
saved in files.

I hope this helps,
Sam Buttrey

messages.body_plain:
Dear Mark,

In my version of S-PLUS (6.2 for Windows), data.frame(cbind(a,b,c,d)) does 
produce a data frame with column names "a", "b", "c", and "d". But why the 
cbind()? If some columns are character data, then this has the effect of 
producing a character matrix, all of the columns of which become factors 
when passed to data.frame(). Is that what you intended? On the other hand, 
data.frame(a,b,c,d) creates a data frame with differentiated columns (also 
named "a", "b", "c", and "d").

By the way, you can assign to names() to change the column names of a data 
frame: e.g., names(df) <- c("A", "B", "C").

I hope this helps,
 John

messages.subject: Re: column naming in dataframe question
messages.body_plain:
First, let me second John Fox's comment; rather than
        data.frame(cbind(a,b,c,d))
use just
        data.frame(a,b,c,d)
Along those lines, if A is a data frame, instead of
        cbind(A, d)
you can do
        data.frame(A, d)
and that this may produce better names (and cbind just calls data.frame anyway).

Second, a possible explanation for the difference between what Leeds and Fox
observed is that
        data.frame(cbind(a,b))
will give names "a" and "b" if cbind(a,b) does so.  That happens if a and b
are ordinary vectors, but not if they are matrices without column names.

Third, here are general rules for names created by data.frame():

Arguments containing a single column:
The order of precedence is:
  * name supplied explicitly
        data.frame(a = x)  # gives name "a"
  * column name supplied by the data.frameAux method (found in the object)
        x <- cbind(b = 1:3)
        data.frame(x)  # gives name "b"
  * name parsed from input
        x <- 1:3
        data.frame(x)  # gives name "x"
  * X1, X2, ...
        data.frame(1:3)

Arguments resulting in multiple columns (e.g. matrices data frames, or lists):
Names include a prefix, in order of precedence:
  * name supplied explicitly
  * name parsed from input
  * X1, X2, ...
and a suffix, in order of precedence:
  * column names supplied by the data.frameAux method 
    (e.g. column names for a matrix),
  * 1, 2, ... 
If no prefix is supplied and an object contains column
names, then no prefix is used.
When both prefix and suffix are present they are separated by ".".

Duplicate names are changed so all names are unique.
as.data.frame uses name "X", rather than "X1".

messages.subject_clean: Saving intermediate values while running scripts
messages.body_plain:
Dear list members:

 

Is it possible, while running a script, to make immediate assignments to variables such that if the script encounters an error at some later point, all intermediate results are not lost?

 

For example: I have three variables, var1 = 0, var2 = 0, and var3 =0, which have been previously defined and are ?sitting? in the current object explorer, with the above assigned values.

 

If I run the following code in a script window:

 

var1 = 1

var2 = 2

var3 = 3

 

Then var1, var2 and var3 will each change to the appropriate value as defined by the script.

 

However, if I run the following script instead of the above script:

 

var1 = 1

var2 = 2

error

var3 = 3

 

The script ?justifiably? aborts with the message ?object ?error? not found. However, var1 and var2 will still be equal to their orginal prescript values ie 0.

 

What I am seeking is a way of running the script so that intermediate assignments to variables are saved so that if the script encounters an error further along all is not lost.

 

Can anyone help?

 

Thanks in advance.

 

Lina

messages.subject: Re: Saving intermediate values while running scripts
messages.subject_clean: Saving intermediate values while running scripts
messages.body_plain:
Something like:

 

 assign("var1", var1, w = 1, 
immediate=T)
assign("var2", var2, w = 1, 
immediate=T)
assign("var3", var3, w = 1, 
immediate=T)

 

saves the results, but by writing them to your working 
directory. So you need to think about the variable names to avoid overwriting 
objects you want preserved. An alternative might be to increment a vector or 
list with successive results, repeatedly assigning the same object (only one 
object name, but can be slow if doing a lot of iterative computing. And I think 
you must be using loops, or any intermediate results of a script would be saved 
anyway (just any intermediate results within a loop within the script would be 
lost upon an error). Depending on how demanding of resources your job is, you 
may want to consider an approach using the 'try' function. This is especially 
useful if you have a few specific types of errors to deal with, so you can write 
followup code to identify when and what error occurred, and what you want to do 
about it. This has the possible advantage of letting your script continue 
after an error occurs, such that needn't assign objects permanently to your 
working directory.

messages.subject: Density Estimation in p dimensions
messages.body_plain:
Many thanks to all that replied.  However no practical solutions were offered, so I devised one that seems to work very well on my data set.

 

Several people stated that the problem was "very difficult" or "infeasible", Hastie et al. (The Elements of Statistical Learning). The book quotes Bellman's "curse of dimensionality" remark in this regard.  But from first hand experience I know Bellman did not regard local estimates and especially mode finding as generally infeasible at p around 10 .

 

The following 2 step process appears to work fine on my problem, ( but I have only began to explore the problem)

 

    1) Reduce the dimensionality if possible. Simply compute the correlation matrix with the data at hand and eliminate all dimensions that have smaller absolute correlations in their off-diagonal elements.

 

    2) Then apply this simple Algo ( and it can be easily extended to find multiple modes if you believe they may exist)

 

           a) Let x(i,j) represent the ith coordinate of the jth point and xbar the corresponding mean then; j ={1,n), j = {1,p} 

               find  j* = arg{ Inf [{j}, Sum(i) [norm(2)( x(i,j) - xbar(j) )/h(i) )] ] }

  where, following Venables and Ripley's suggestion in MASS (4th ed) p. 127 

   h(i) = 0.9* Inter-Quartile-Range(x(i,.)/1.34 * n^(-0.2)
 

        ( This really amounts to a kernal  MLE gaussian fit )

 

        b)  Calculate n-3  new points  ( for n even) in the range[ x(i, j*-n/2), x(i, j*+n/2) ] 

 

         c) Loop: go to a) and repeat, Stop when the difference in values of norm*   from      the last iteration  < tol

 

    My first efforts with this require only a few iterations to obtain a good mode if you are fortunate enough to start with a well-spread set of x's.

 

This is not a strictly S+ or R problem but rather a statistical estimation problem - - -  perhaps someone has some idea of how to solve the problem.

 

   I have a p dimension vector where p maybe as large as 10 to 20, and I have m samples of the vector  each obtained via a time-consuming calculation; m maybe as large as 20 to 50.

 

   Problem: Assume that the distribution of the vector is uni-modal, How do I estimate the location of the mode ?  How do I estimate the density of the vector? 

 

     Grid search is not an option because of the high dimensionality.  The samples cannot be selected at given points in p-space, so I cannot utilize a conventional Newton-Raphson search process.  Perhaps a p dimensional version of  a Brent polynomial process ( the one dimensional version is employed in function uniroot) would work.  Does such a routine exist ?

 

Paul Lasky

B & P Consultants

messages.body_plain:
Thank you to all of you that replied.

The result can certainly be achieved with a "for" loop:

mat0 <- matrix(0, ncol=p, nrow=p)
for (i in length(list)) mat0 <- mat0 + list[[i]]

but two other solutions has been suggested, where the idea is to use 
unlist(). I suspect that both these options are faster than the loop.

------------------------------------------------------------------------------ 

p <- 5

lis <- list(matrix(seq(1, p*p), p, p), matrix(seq(1, p*p), p, p),
matrix(seq(1, p*p), p, p))

####

mat <- matrix(unlist(lis), p*p, length(lis))

mat <- matrix(rowSums(mat), p, p)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

m.array <- array( unlist( m.list), dim = c( p, q, n)) # Assuming m.list is a 
list of n (pxq)-matrices.
apply( m.array, 1:2, sum)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Note that

lapply(your.matrix.list, sum)

doesn't do the the work because it produces a list, where each component 
i is the sum of all the elements of your.matrix.list[[i]].

Eva

messages.subject: Re: apply function
messages.body_plain:
The problem is that you create "testA" as a vector consisting of 
one column from the data.frame MSfactor.  Using "as.array", you force it 
to be an array.  However, it is only a 1-dimensional array.  Then you 
want to sweep out the first dimension, retaining dimension 2.  Since it 
is only a 1-dimensional array, any request for dimension 2 is illegal as 
it does not exist. 

     The simplest fix is to add ", drop=FALSE" to the extraction from 
MSfactor.  Consider the following example: 

MSfactor <- data.frame(a=1:2, b=3:4)
testA <- MSfactor[,2, drop=FALSE]
apply(testA, 2, mean)
 b
3.5

     hope this helps.  spencer graves

p.s.  See e.g., p. 29 of Venables and Ripley (2002) Modern Applied 
Statistics with S (Springer).  I have found this to be a very useful 
book by two of the leaders in statistical computing.

messages.subject: Re: AIC for split-plot ANOVA
messages.body_plain:
That `model' is actually (probably) three models, one for each error
stratum.  There is no overall likelihood being maximized, and hence no AIC
is even defined.

On Tue, 17 Feb 2004, Spencer Graves wrote:

>       "?lme" says, "See lmeObject for the components of the fit."  The 
> latter reveals that the output includes a component "loglik", from which 
> one can compute the AIC.  Pinheiro and Bates (2000) Mixed-Effects Models 
> in S and S-Plus (Springer) discuss how to use this function, including 
> how to get various types of plots. 
> 
>       hope this helps.  spencer graves

He is calling aov, not lme.  The aov fit is equivalent to an lme REML fit, 
not an lme ML fit which would be needed to compute a value for AIC.

The function AIC will give you a value for a default lme fit, but it is 
not of Akaike's AIC.

> Christoph Scherber wrote:
> 
> > Dear all,
> >
> > is it possible to calculate the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) for 
> > a split-plot ANOVA model in S-Plus?
> >
> > the model looks like model1_aov(response~factors+Error(Plot/Treatment))
> >
> > Additionally, I´d like to know how to produce diagnostic plots (Q-Q 
> > plots, Residuals etc) for that kind of model.

You do it by stratum: see the examples in MASS (Venables & Ripley, 2002 
and earlier).

messages.subject: Re: SUMMARY: How to sum (matrix) components of a list?
messages.subject_clean: SUMMARY: How to sum (matrix) components of a list?
messages.body_plain:
>>> I do have a list where each component is a  p x p matrix. I'm unable 
>>> to find a way to sum these matrices. Any idea?

Three comments on summing matrices in a list:

(1) One way is
        matrix( fastRowSums( unlist( myList ), n=p*p ), p )
This is similar to the rowSums solution below, except that fastRowSums
does not require you to turn the vector of length k*p*p into a matrix
(where k = number of matrices) before doing the row sums; instead the
"n=p*p" part says to pretend that this vector is a matrix with p*p rows.

In general fastRowSums and fastColSums take the sums of regularly-spaced
subsets of data.  Similarly for fast{Row,Col}{Means, Vars, Stdevs}.
These are part of the S+Resample library, at
        www.insightful.com/downloads/libraries

(2) In the "apply( m.array, 1:2, sum)" solution, replace the apply call with
        rowSums(m.array, dims=2)
This says to treat the first two dimensions (out of 3) as "row" dimensions.

I strongly encourage everyone to change (almost) all calls to
        apply(..., sum)
        apply(..., mean)
        apply(..., var)
        apply(..., stdev)
with 
        rowSums or colSums
        rowMeans or colMeans
        rowVars or colVars
        rowStdevs or colStdevs
or the fast* variations.  Your code will be faster and more legible.

(3) Two things that do not work in general are:
  (a)   do.call("sum", myList)
  because it produces a single number rather than a matrix, and
  (b)   do.call("+", myList)
  because "+" only accepts two arguments.

I'll also throw in a plug for the courses
        Advanced Programming Methods in S-PLUS
        Bootstrap Methods and Permutation Tests
that I'll teach in March, in Boston and San Francisco; schedule at
        http://www.insightful.com/services/schedule.asp

messages.subject: Re: transpose a data frame
messages.body_plain:
Dear Joe,

t() works on data frames, so all you need do is t(your.data.frame). Of 
course, this likely only makes sense if all of the columns of 
your.data.frame are numeric, and a numeric matrix will result. If you want 
the transpose to be a data frame, then you can do 
as.data.frame(t(your.data.frame)).

You can remove the column names from a data frame by names(my.data.frame) 
<- NULL, but that seems to me generally ill-advised.

I hope this helps,
 John

messages.subject: Re: NLME loop termination
messages.body_plain:
Usually
    try(expr)
takes care of this kind of problem.  If the expression fails,
try takes care of loose ends and continues with the loop.
If you "try" to do an assignment and it fails, the old value
stays in the to assign variable (which is convenient if it was
NA to start with) and the loop continues.  At the end you
can see how many failed to complete.

Check the documentation on "try".

Pete

messages.body_plain:
On Fri, 20 Feb 2004 Jo.Jiao at csiro.au wrote:

> Hi, here is a simple question about linear regression. Just say I have
> fitted a simple regression model: y=b0 + b1*X The estimates of b0 and
> b1are bo_hat and b1_hat. I have noted that the fitted values calculated
> using the function fitted.values are differenct from those calculated
> using bo_hat+ b1_hat*X . The difference between the two kinds of fitted
> values is not big, but I suppose they shall be exactly the same. Can
> someone give me a clue?

You are doing a numerical calculation two different ways, so I would not 
expect them to be _exactly_ the same.  Did you use the coefficients as 
printed, or the stored values?  (The printed values are rounded.)

It helps enormously to give an example of such a claim.  Here is my 
attempt to reproduce it:

> x <- 1:25
> y <- 10+x+rnorm(25)
> fit <- lm(y ~ x)
> fit
Call:
lm(formula = y ~ x)

Coefficients:
 (Intercept)        x
    10.09406 1.002956

Degrees of freedom: 25 total; 23 residual
Residual standard error: 1.038494
> z <- drop(cbind(1, x) %*% coef(fit))
> range(z - fitted(fit))
[1] 0.00000e+00 1.24345e-14

so the numbers differ by around the precision of the calculations
(.Machine$double.eps times their size).

--

messages.subject: Re: Understanding Self Start Function for Asymptotic
messages.subject_clean: Understanding Self Start Function for Asymptotic
messages.body_plain:
jrausch at nd.edu writes:

> Regarding my first question, 
> 
> I would like to thank Bert Gunter, Sam Buttrey, Scott Chasalow, and Patrick
> Burns, all who alerted me to the fact that I need to call upon
> "NLSstRtAsymptote.sortedXyData" to determine the algorithm for the
> NLSstRtAsymptote() function.
> 
> With respect to the second question (which can be found at the bottom of this
> email) regarding the nls.control() option when using the SSasymp self-start
> function within nls(), I would greatly appreciate any leads/suggestions for
> determining the answer to this. 

If you want to have complete control you can avoid the selfStart
function entirely and determine your own starting estimates for the
parameters.  Because the asymptotic regression model has two
conditionally linear parameters and only one nonlinear parameters, you
only need to specify one starting estimate (the rate constant) if you
use algorithm = "plinear" in a call to nls.  As the model only makes
sense for positive rate constants we use the logarithm of the rate
constant (lrc).

That's exactly what is occuring when you get the error message

Error in nls(y ~ cbind(1 - exp(-exp(lrc) * x), exp(-exp(lrc) * x)), data = 
xy,  : step factor 0.000488281 reduced below `minFactor' of 0.000976563

If that optimization fails then changing the minimum step factor won't
help you.  Failure of this one-parameter optimization indicates that
for some reason your data cannot be fit by the model.  I suggest that
you plot your data and look at them carefully.  If, for example, your
data are exactly linear, then you won't be able to fit the asymptotic
regression model.

You can perform an equivalent optimization, including a trace of the
optimization steps, using

nls(Y ~ cbind(1, exp(-exp(lrc) * x)), start = c(lrc = -0.1), alg =
"plinear", trace = TRUE)

Look to see what the values of lrc are doing.  If they are going to
negative infinity then you are not going to be able to fit this model
to these data.

-- 
Douglas Bates                            bates at stat.wisc.edu
Statistics Department                    608/262-2598
University of Wisconsin - Madison        http://www.stat.wisc.edu/~bates/

> Does anyone experience this problem in using "S+BEST" library -- the 
> library to fit Hazard Regression (HARE) model? In the window setting (with

The S+BEST library only works with S-PLUS for Windows 6.0 or later (6.0,
6.1 or 6.2). This is noted on the Research Libraries web page
(http://www.insightful.com/downloads/libraries/default.asp) but the note
can easily be overlooked. I will update the web page to make it obvious
which version of S-PLUS is required for each of the libraries.

messages.subject: ancova model checking
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have several partially correlated explanatory variables that I want to 
analyse using analysis of covariance. 

The problem now is that order in model specification matters. I would 
therefore like to have an automated routine which permutates the 
positions of the explanatory variables, and then compares all resulting 
model versions using AIC.

What I´d like to do is something like:

explanatories_c(explanatory.1,explanatory.2,explanatory.3....explanatory.n)
for (i in 1:n) explanatory[i]_sample((explanatories[i])
model[i]_aov(response~explanatory[i])
AIC(model[i+1],model[i])

this whole procedure would then be replicated until the full nr of 
explanatory variables (say, 10) is tested in all possible positions 
(e.g. 10!)

I would really appreciate any suggestions on this.

Best regards
Christoph.

There are faster systematic ways to go about this, but any of these
procedures are likely to destroy the meaning of P-values, confidence
limits, and result in biased regression models with overly optimistic R^2
and betas.  If you are doing ANCOVA in order to test for a treatment
effect you are really in trouble.  Pre-specify the model.

 The ECML/PKDD-2004 organizing committee invites proposals for

 Workshops provide organizers and participants with an opportunity to

 communities could be the focus of a workshop. Workshops can

messages.subject: Loess span optimization: calculating AIC.
messages.body_plain:
Good Day,

I am looking for a way to optimize selection of span for a loess model in S-Plus. Any options out there?

One option I am having trouble with…

The SAS documentation provides a macro that uses the unbiased AIC to optimize residual error and span.

Ref: Cohen, RA. Paper 273, An Introduction to PROC LOESS for Local Regression.

I am having difficulty porting this to S as I cannot identify all of the terms from the loess model.

Here is the theoretical model provided in the reference, it is to be calculated for each value of span.

AIC <- (n*(sigma.hat^2)) + (n*(((delta.1)/(delta.2*(n + traceL)))/((delta.1^2)/(delta.2 - 2))))

Terms required, the ones I am not sure of have question marks. Advide on identifying these terms would be appreciated.

n:  obvious

traceL:  loess.model$inference$trace.hat?

delta1:  loess.model$inference$one.delta

delta2:  loess.model$inference$two.delta

sigma.hat^2: loess.model$inference$s^2?

The macro calculation provided in the reference is not exactly like the one above, it is as follows and includes terms from the ODS output from SAS.

sigmaHat = rss/n

AIC = n*log(sigmaHat) + ((delta1/delta2)*(n+nul)/(lkdf-2))

Additional terms in the SAS macro by Cohen

rss(residual sum of squares): sum(loess.model$residual^2)?

nul: ???

lkdf(lookup degrees of freedom): ??? not same as enp

What are these extra terms that are not in the theoretical model?

S-Plus function:
World    World Map

USAGE
map('world')

This world database comes from a cleaned-up version of the
CIA World Data Bank II data and contains approximately 2 million
points representing the world coastlines and national boundaries.
This makes it suitable for extracting countries, continents, etc
while still retaining lots of detail.
This size also makes the world database unsuitable for drawing

messages.body_plain:
Ernst,

I don't have any solution for your problem directly, but (worse), I'd like
to warn you against such importance measure for some data sets.  This type
of measures can be very misleading if the predictor variables used in the
tree have very different number of possible splits.  (This description might
sound strange, but that's the fact.)  For a numerical variable, the number
of possible split is the number of unique values minus 1.  For a categorical
variable, the number of possible splits is the number of ways to divide the
categories into two non-empty groups.

The gist of the problem is this: most tree induction algorithms have the
problem of `preferring' to split on variables with larger number of possible
splits.  Given two predictors with same correlation with the response, tree
will tend to split on the one with more possible splits.  The net effect is
that the measure you mention will make variables with larger number of
possible splits look more important than they really are.

(Some authors have tried to modify splitting procedures to `correct the
bias', but they all have their own problems...)

Best,
Andy

Brent,

set.seed(1)
tmp <- data.frame(x = sort(runif(100)))
tmp$y <- cos(2 * pi * tmp$x) + exp(tmp$x) + rnorm(nrow(tmp))

fit <- loess(y ~ x, data = tmp, span = 0.1)
rss <- sum(residuals(fit)^2)
for(sp in seq(0.2, 1, 0.1)) {
  fit <- update(fit, span = sp)
  rss <- c(rss, sum(residuals(fit)^2))

messages.subject: Re: Q: How can I get a complete sequence of sub-trees and their
messages.subject_clean: Q: How can I get a complete sequence of sub-trees and their
messages.body_plain:
Dear S-Plus users:

I was able to solve my problem.  In short, I needed the "snip.tree" command
rather than the "prune.tree" command.
I enclose my function below, for anyone interested.

Andy Liaw pointed out that the relative measures of importance of variables
based on deviance reduction by internal splits in a tree
should be used with caution. In particular, if the input variables
for a tree are of mixed type (eg continuous versus categorical) such
measure may be severely biased since one type of variable may
favor more splits than the other type.

Thanks again,

Ernst.

# Calculates relative importance of variables in a tree
# Provides a table (vector) of the contribution of each variable
rel.impo <- function(tree1)
{
# Sequence of internal nodes
intern.fr <- tree1$frame[tree1$frame$var != '<leaf>',]
nodes <- row.names(intern.fr)
vars <- as.character(intern.fr$var)
n.intern <- nrow(intern.fr)

# Calculate deviance of recursively snipped subtrees
devs <- rep(deviance(tree1),(n.intern+1))
for (i in 2 : n.intern)
       devs[i] <- deviance(snip.tree(tree1,nodes=nodes[(n.intern+2-i)]))
devs[n.intern+1] <- tree1$frame$dev[1]

# Calculate differences in deviances and rearrange terms in correct sequence
impo <- diff(devs)
vars <- vars[n.intern : 1]

tapply(impo,vars,sum)
}

messages.subject: Re: Levene test
messages.body_plain:
Dear Chris,

The following function is from my Rcmdr package for R, and is a slightly 
modified version of a solution contributed by Brian Ripley to the R-help list:

levene.test <- function(y, group) {
    meds <- tapply(y, group, median, na.rm=TRUE)
    resp <- abs(y - meds[group])
    table <- anova(lm(resp ~ group, na.action=na.omit))
    rownames(table)[2] <- " "
    cat("Levene's Test for Homogeneity of Variance\n\n")
    table[,c(1,4,5)]
    }

For S-PLUS, I've changed the function to specify na.action=na.omit in the 
call to lm().

I hope this helps,
 John

messages.body_plain:
Dear users of S-news

As part of a function I would like to calculate transpose(A) %*% A so that 
the first row of transpose(A) is matched with the 1st row of A. The second 
row of Transpose(A) is matched with the second column of A, etc.

For example if:

A =     1 2 3
        4 5 6

Then the operation would return

transpose(A) %*% A =    14
                                77

I have used three methods on an example where A is an 18x900 matrix:

1. Apply:               e.g.    apply(A,2,function(A)t(A)%*%A))

Dos time of function = 4.736s

2. For loop:            e.g.    for( i in 1: x){test[i]<-t(A[,i])%*%A[,i]}

Dos time of function = 4.837s

3. Matrix multiplication:       e.g.    diag(t(test)%*%test)

Dos time of function = 1.181s

If I don't do this part of the procedure and use a made-up matrix for A 
then the Dos time of the function is 0.531s.

I would like the function to run as quickly as possible to use in 
resampling.  I have the feeling that there must be a better way to do this 
than method 3. If anyone has encountered this problem before I would be 
happy to hear if there is a better way.

It should not need any description: it is the rbind method for objects of
class Matrix, and it works by unpacking Matrix objects to matrices.  
Please do read the White Book about S3 generic functions and their
methods.  You shoul dnot be calling methods directly except in very
special circumstances.

> the function "rbind" and to use instead "rbind.Matrix" which is faster for
> very large data frames.

All you are doing is converting data frames to matrices, and it may be 
faster but at the expense of not doing the important part of the 
computations, matching up the column types in A and B.

> Let's consider the simplified example:
> 
> A<-data.frame(Fact=LETTERS[1:3],NR=1:3)         ## 3x3-data.frame
> B<-data.frame(Fact=LETTERS[1:2],NR=1:2)         ## 2x3-data.frame
> 
> C1<-rbind(A,B)
> > C1
>   Fact NR
> 1    A  1
> 2    B  2
> 3    C  3
> 4    D  1
> 5    E  2
> 
> library(Matrix)
> C2<-rbind.Matrix(A,B)
> > C2
>           Fact         NR
> [1,] factor, 3 numeric, 3
> [2,] factor, 2 numeric, 2
> attr(, "class"):
> [1] "Matrix"
> 
> Is there any Splus-function (or other possibilities except for loops) which
> enables to generate the data frame C1 from C2?

You don't want to do that!  It may well be faster to set up a data frame 
of the right size and type and assign blocks of rows.  E.g.

AB <- A[rep(1, nrow(A) + nrow(B)), ]
AB[1:nrow(A),] <- A
AB[nrow(A) + 1:nrow(B),] <- B

especially if this is being done for many data frames.

expectancy effects by 
Raudenbush):

Data meta;

'c:\meta.txt';

Invsd=1/(sd);

messages.body_plain:
This is what I'm trying to do in S-Plus, using the GUI interface.

Again, here's the SAS code:

Data meta;
    Infile 'c:\meta.txt';
    Input effect sd week studyID;
    Invsd=1/(sd);
    Run;

Proc mixed covtest data=meta;
    Class studyID;
    Weight invsd;
    Model effect = week /s;
    Random int /type=un sub=studyID;
    Parms (0.1) (1)/hold=(2);
    Run;

And here's what I'm doing in S-Plus GUI.

First, I load the spreadsheet into the GUI.  The data is in columns, in the
following order:

studyid  effect  sd  week   invsd

I go up to "Statistics", then choose "Mixed effects", then "Linear."

Data set is "Raudenbush"

In "Fixed effects", I choose effect as the dependent.  For "independent", I
choose week.  This results in the formula:

effect~week

In "Random effects", I choose "studyid" as a group variable.  This creates
the random formula ~1 | studyid

I then click "Options."

I choose "Within group variance" as "Fixed."

I choose "Invsd" as the covariate since this is the weight variable.

I choose "Within group correlation" as "General Symmetric"

Group variable as "studyid"

Not sure what to put for parameters...I put "1" because I want to hold the
lowest covariance structure as with the SAS code, but I don't know if I'm
doing this correctly.

When I run the stats, I get an error message that says:

"Problem in varFixed: argument form= not matched: varFixed(form = ~invsd, )

I can't seem to figure out how to implement the above SAS code into
equivalent S-Plus code.

James

messages.subject: How to find the dates?
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

I have a very large cohort data that contains repeated measures. The 
data looks like:

id   days  event
1     0     0
1    30     0
1    50     0
1    95     1
1   120     1
1   147     0
1   180     0
2     0     0
2    75     0
2   100     0
3     0     0
3    37     1
3    80     1

I need help in finding the following survival times:
 1. For each subject, find the first day that event=1.
 2. If a subject never has event=1, then the last day is used with
    an indicator of censoring (say, censor=1).

For the above data, I expect to obtain:

id  days  censor
1    95      0
2   100      1
3    37      0

The next question bothers me more. Now I restrict to only subjects who 
have ever had event=1 (in this example, only subjects 1 and 3). How can 
I find the how many days it takes for the subject to return to event=0? 
As before, if a subject never returns to event=0, the last observation 
day is used with an indicator of censoring. In the above data, I expect 
to get

id  days  censor
1   52     0
3   43     1

Many thanks!

Regards,
Peng Huang

You will get prod(dim(M)-1) 3-dimensional arrays.  What do you want 
to do with these 3-d arrays?  At least at the prototype stage, I might 
use "for" loops. 

> M <- array(1:27, dim = c(3, 3, 3))
> M.sum <- array(NA, dim = dim(M) - 1)
> for(i in 1:2)
   for(j in 1:2)
       for(k in 1:2)
           M.sum[i, j, k] <- M[ - c(i, i + 1),  - c(j, j + 1),
                - c(k, k + 1)]
> M
